claim: YAP and TAZ are essential for Schwann cells to develop, maintain and regenerate myelin.
source: Previously we showed that the hippo pathway transcriptional effectors, YAP and TAZ, are essential for Schwann cells (SCs) to develop, maintain and regenerate myelin
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TEAD1 has been implicated as a partner transcription factor for YAP/TAZ.
source: Although TEAD1 has been implicated as a partner transcription factor, the mechanisms by which it mediates YAP/TAZ regulation of SC myelination are unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge in the field.

claim: TEAD1 is crucial for Schwann cells to develop myelin.
source: Here, using conditional and inducible knockout mice, we show that TEAD1 is crucial for SCs to develop and regenerate myelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from conditional and inducible knockout mice presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEAD1 is crucial for Schwann cells to regenerate myelin.
source: Here, using conditional and inducible knockout mice, we show that TEAD1 is crucial for SCs to develop and regenerate myelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from conditional and inducible knockout mice presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEAD1 promotes myelination by positively regulating Schwann cell proliferation.
source: It promotes myelination by both positively and negatively regulating SC proliferation, enabling Krox20/Egr2 to upregulate myelin proteins, and upregulating the cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes FDPS and IDI1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on SC proliferation at different developmental stages presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEAD1 promotes myelination by negatively regulating Schwann cell proliferation.
source: It promotes myelination by both positively and negatively regulating SC proliferation, enabling Krox20/Egr2 to upregulate myelin proteins, and upregulating the cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes FDPS and IDI1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on SC proliferation at different developmental stages presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEAD1 enables Krox20/Egr2 to upregulate myelin proteins.
source: It promotes myelination by both positively and negatively regulating SC proliferation, enabling Krox20/Egr2 to upregulate myelin proteins, and upregulating the cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes FDPS and IDI1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Krox20 expression and myelin protein levels in Tead1 cKO mice.

claim: TEAD1 upregulates the cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme FDPS.
source: It promotes myelination by both positively and negatively regulating SC proliferation, enabling Krox20/Egr2 to upregulate myelin proteins, and upregulating the cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes FDPS and IDI1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced FDPS levels in Tead1 cKO mice.

claim: TEAD1 upregulates the cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme IDI1.
source: It promotes myelination by both positively and negatively regulating SC proliferation, enabling Krox20/Egr2 to upregulate myelin proteins, and upregulating the cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes FDPS and IDI1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced IDI1 levels in Tead1 cKO mice.

claim: There is stage-dependent redundancy of TEAD1 in Schwann cells.
source: We also show stage-dependent redundancy of TEAD1 and that non-myelinating SCs have a unique requirement for TEAD1 to enwrap nociceptive axons in Remak bundles.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing phenotypes of Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO mice at different developmental stages.

claim: Non-myelinating Schwann cells have a unique requirement for TEAD1 to enwrap nociceptive axons in Remak bundles.
source: We also show stage-dependent redundancy of TEAD1 and that non-myelinating SCs have a unique requirement for TEAD1 to enwrap nociceptive axons in Remak bundles.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis of Remak bundles in Tead1 cKO and iKO mice.

claim: TEAD1 is a major partner of YAP/TAZ in developmental myelination.
source: Our findings establish TEAD1 as a major partner of YAP/TAZ in developmental myelination and functional nerve regeneration and as a novel transcription factor regulating Remak bundle integrity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the similarity of phenotypes between Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO mice.

claim: TEAD1 is a major partner of YAP/TAZ in functional nerve regeneration.
source: Our findings establish TEAD1 as a major partner of YAP/TAZ in developmental myelination and functional nerve regeneration and as a novel transcription factor regulating Remak bundle integrity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing failure of remyelination in Tead1 iKO mice after nerve crush.

claim: TEAD1 is a novel transcription factor regulating Remak bundle integrity.
source: Our findings establish TEAD1 as a major partner of YAP/TAZ in developmental myelination and functional nerve regeneration and as a novel transcription factor regulating Remak bundle integrity.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM analysis showing defective C-fiber ensheathment in Tead1 cKO and iKO mice.

claim: Axons larger than 1 μm diameter are enveloped by myelinating Schwann cells that form multilamellar myelin sheaths.
source: Axons larger than 1 μm diameter are enveloped by myelinating SCs that form multilamellar myelin sheaths with a thickness proportional to axon caliber (Jessen and Mirsky, 2005; Salzer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established knowledge in the field.

claim: Myelin sheath thickness is proportional to axon caliber.
source: Axons larger than 1 μm diameter are enveloped by myelinating SCs that form multilamellar myelin sheaths with a thickness proportional to axon caliber (Jessen and Mirsky, 2005; Salzer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established knowledge in the field.

claim: Axons smaller than 1 μm diameter are organized in clusters called Remak bundles.
source: Axons smaller than 1 μm diameter, the unmyelinated nociceptors (i.e., C-fibers), are organized in clusters called Remak bundles, in which each C-fiber is ensheathed by a cytoplasmic pocket formed by non-myelinating SCs, also known as Remak SCs (Beirowski et al., 2014; Harty and Monk, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established knowledge in the field.

claim: In Remak bundles, each C-fiber is ensheathed by a cytoplasmic pocket formed by non-myelinating Schwann cells.
source: Axons smaller than 1 μm diameter, the unmyelinated nociceptors (i.e., C-fibers), are organized in clusters called Remak bundles, in which each C-fiber is ensheathed by a cytoplasmic pocket formed by non-myelinating SCs, also known as Remak SCs (Beirowski et al., 2014; Harty and Monk, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established knowledge in the field.

claim: Both myelinating and non-myelinating Schwann cells provide metabolic and functional support essential for structural and functional integrity of peripheral nerves.
source: Both myelinating and non-myelinating SCs provide metabolic and functional support essential for structural and functional integrity of peripheral nerves.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Failure to initiate or maintain proper axon-Schwann cell association may lead to life-threatening paralysis and peripheral neuropathy.
source: Failure to initiate or maintain proper axon-SC association may lead to life-threatening paralysis and peripheral neuropathy (Scherer and Wrabetz, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge in the field.

claim: Myelinating Schwann cells form and maintain myelin via a set of key transcription factors and regulators.
source: Myelinating SCs form and maintain myelin via a set of key transcription factors (TFs) and regulators (Bremer et al., 2011; Decker et al., 2006; Finzsch et al., 2010; He et al., 2010; Jaegle et al., 2003; Kao et al., 2009; Le et al., 2005a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established knowledge in the field.

claim: The transcriptional regulation of myelinating Schwann cells remains incompletely understood.
source: However, the transcriptional regulation of myelinating SCs remains incompletely understood, and that of non-myelinating SCs is largely unknown (Harty and Monk, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge in the field.

claim: The transcriptional regulation of non-myelinating Schwann cells is largely unknown.
source: However, the transcriptional regulation of myelinating SCs remains incompletely understood, and that of non-myelinating SCs is largely unknown (Harty and Monk, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge in the field.

claim: YAP and TAZ play crucial roles in developing, maintaining, and regenerating myelination of peripheral nerves.
source: Recent mouse genetic studies surprisingly revealed that YAP (Yes-associated protein, also known as YAP1) and its paralogue, TAZ (Transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif, also known as WWTR1), which are potent oncoproteins and transcriptional regulators in the Hippo signaling pathway, play crucial roles in developing, maintaining, and regenerating myelination of peripheral nerves.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent mouse genetic studies.

claim: YAP and TAZ are expressed initially in all immature Schwann cells and then selectively in myelinating Schwann cells.
source: Both YAP and TAZ (YAP/TAZ) are expressed initially in all immature SCs and then selectively in myelinating SCs (Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for timely sorting of large axons and associated Schwann cell proliferation.
source: The processes for which they are required include: timely sorting of large axons and associated SC proliferation (Grove et al., 2017; Poitelon et al., 2016); initiation of SC differentiation or myelination (Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017); myelin maintenance in adults Grove et al., 2017; and remyelination following nerve injury (Grove et al., 2020; Jeanette et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for initiation of Schwann cell differentiation or myelination.
source: The processes for which they are required include: timely sorting of large axons and associated SC proliferation (Grove et al., 2017; Poitelon et al., 2016); initiation of SC differentiation or myelination (Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017); myelin maintenance in adults Grove et al., 2017; and remyelination following nerve injury (Grove et al., 2020; Jeanette et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for myelin maintenance in adults.
source: The processes for which they are required include: timely sorting of large axons and associated SC proliferation (Grove et al., 2017; Poitelon et al., 2016); initiation of SC differentiation or myelination (Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017); myelin maintenance in adults Grove et al., 2017; and remyelination following nerve injury (Grove et al., 2020; Jeanette et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for remyelination following nerve injury.
source: The processes for which they are required include: timely sorting of large axons and associated SC proliferation (Grove et al., 2017; Poitelon et al., 2016); initiation of SC differentiation or myelination (Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017); myelin maintenance in adults Grove et al., 2017; and remyelination following nerve injury (Grove et al., 2020; Jeanette et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP/TAZ initiate and maintain myelination in part by upregulating Krox20.
source: YAP/TAZ initiate and maintain myelination in part by upregulating Krox20 (Egr2; Grove et al., 2017; Lopez-Anido et al., 2016), which is widely recognized as the master TF promoting peripheral myelination by SCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Krox20 is widely recognized as the master transcription factor promoting peripheral myelination by Schwann cells.
source: YAP/TAZ initiate and maintain myelination in part by upregulating Krox20 (Egr2; Grove et al., 2017; Lopez-Anido et al., 2016), which is widely recognized as the master TF promoting peripheral myelination by SCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Krox20 is required to develop and maintain myelin.
source: Krox20 is required to develop and maintain myelin (Decker et al., 2006; Topilko et al., 1994), and likely to promote myelin sheath growth (Le et al., 2005a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Krox20 likely promotes myelin sheath growth.
source: Krox20 is required to develop and maintain myelin (Decker et al., 2006; Topilko et al., 1994), and likely to promote myelin sheath growth (Le et al., 2005a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study and involves speculation.

claim: Krox20 acts through direct transcriptional upregulation of myelin proteins and membrane lipids.
source: It acts through direct transcriptional upregulation of myelin proteins and membrane lipids (Jang et al., 2010; Jang and Svaren, 2009; LeBlanc et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP/TAZ are transcriptional co-activators that contain a transcriptional activation domain, but no DNA binding domain.
source: YAP/TAZ are transcriptional co-activators that contain a transcriptional activation domain, but no DNA binding domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: YAP/TAZ regulate gene expression by binding to partner transcription factors, typically members of the TEA domain family (TEAD1-4).
source: They regulate gene expression by binding to partner TFs, typically members of the TEA domain family (TEAD1-4; Wu et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TEADs on their own are unable to activate or repress transcription and require the help of co-factors such as YAP/TAZ to act.
source: Conversely, TEADs on their own are unable to activate or repress transcription and require the help of co-factors such as YAP/TAZ to act (Li et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Partner transcription factors such as TEADs are required to maintain YAP/TAZ in the nucleus, which keeps them transcriptionally active.
source: Partner TFs such as TEADs are required to maintain YAP/TAZ in the nucleus, which keeps them transcriptionally active (Diepenbruck et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2020; Kofler et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Schwann cells express all four TEADs (TEAD1/2/3/4).
source: Recent single-cell transcriptional analysis indicates that SCs express all four TEADs (TEAD1/2/3/4) and that their expression peaks at different times during development (Gerber et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent single-cell transcriptional analysis.

claim: TEAD expression peaks at different times during Schwann cell development.
source: Recent single-cell transcriptional analysis indicates that SCs express all four TEADs (TEAD1/2/3/4) and that their expression peaks at different times during development (Gerber et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent single-cell transcriptional analysis.

claim: TEAD1-4 show unique, redundant, and/or opposing roles in regulating proliferation and differentiation of various cell types.
source: Moreover, TEAD1-4 show unique, redundant, and/or opposing roles in regulating proliferation and differentiation of various cell types; these roles can also change as a function of developmental stage (He et al., 2018; Mukhtar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The roles of TEAD1-4 can change as a function of developmental stage.
source: Moreover, TEAD1-4 show unique, redundant, and/or opposing roles in regulating proliferation and differentiation of various cell types; these roles can also change as a function of developmental stage (He et al., 2018; Mukhtar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In some cell types, TEAD1 serves as the main partner TEAD and plays non-redundant roles.
source: In some cell types, TEAD1 serves as the main partner TEAD and plays non-redundant roles (Liu et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In Schwann cells, TEAD1 associates with YAP/TAZ for upregulating myelin proteins.
source: In accordance, in SCs, TEAD1 associates with YAP/TAZ for upregulating myelin proteins as indicated by ChiP, co-IP, and transcription assays (Fernando et al., 2016; Grove et al., 2017; Lopez-Anido et al., 2016; Lopez-Anido et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using ChIP, co-IP, and transcription assays.

claim: Unlike YAP/TAZ, which are barely detectable in non-myelinating Schwann cells, TEAD1 is clearly expressed in all Schwann cell nuclei.
source: Notably, however, unlike YAP/TAZ, which are barely detectable in non-myelinating SCs, TEAD1 is clearly expressed in all SC nuclei (Grove et al., 2017), suggesting that, independently of YAP/TAZ, TEAD1 plays an unknown role in non-myelinating SCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: TEAD1 plays an unknown role in non-myelinating Schwann cells independently of YAP/TAZ.
source: Notably, however, unlike YAP/TAZ, which are barely detectable in non-myelinating SCs, TEAD1 is clearly expressed in all SC nuclei (Grove et al., 2017), suggesting that, independently of YAP/TAZ, TEAD1 plays an unknown role in non-myelinating SCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential expression pattern of TEAD1 vs YAP/TAZ in non-myelinating SCs.

claim: TEAD1 was expressed in the nuclei of 100% of WT Schwann cells at P22.
source: Immunostaining of P22 WT and Mpz-Cre;Tead1fl/fl (hereafter Tead1 cKO) sciatic nerves (SNs) showed that TEAD1 was expressed in the nuclei of 100% of WT SCs and was undetectable in >97% Tead1 cKO SCs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TEAD1 was undetectable in >97% of Tead1 cKO Schwann cells at P22.
source: Immunostaining of P22 WT and Mpz-Cre;Tead1fl/fl (hereafter Tead1 cKO) sciatic nerves (SNs) showed that TEAD1 was expressed in the nuclei of 100% of WT SCs and was undetectable in >97% Tead1 cKO SCs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Loss of TEAD1 does not affect nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ in Schwann cells.
source: Indeed, YAP/TAZ were retained in the SC nucleus of Tead1 cKO (Figure 1D), presumably due to other TEADs in the absence of TEAD1.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Other TEADs retain YAP/TAZ in the nucleus in the absence of TEAD1.
source: Indeed, YAP/TAZ were retained in the SC nucleus of Tead1 cKO (Figure 1D), presumably due to other TEADs in the absence of TEAD1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that YAP/TAZ remain nuclear despite loss of TEAD1.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice were smaller than WT mice at all ages.
source: Tead1 cKO mice were smaller than WT mice at all ages, with labored breathing and widely splayed fore- and hindlimbs, indicative of severe peripheral neuropathy (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of mice shown in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibited labored breathing.
source: Tead1 cKO mice were smaller than WT mice at all ages, with labored breathing and widely splayed fore- and hindlimbs, indicative of severe peripheral neuropathy (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of mice shown in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibited widely splayed fore- and hindlimbs.
source: Tead1 cKO mice were smaller than WT mice at all ages, with labored breathing and widely splayed fore- and hindlimbs, indicative of severe peripheral neuropathy (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of mice shown in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: The phenotype of Tead1 cKO mice is indicative of severe peripheral neuropathy.
source: Tead1 cKO mice were smaller than WT mice at all ages, with labored breathing and widely splayed fore- and hindlimbs, indicative of severe peripheral neuropathy (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the observed phenotype based on established knowledge.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice were humanely euthanized before P60 because of neuropathy.
source: Because of the neuropathy, Tead1 cKO mice were humanely euthanized before P60.
evidence: This is a statement of experimental procedure.

claim: Tead1 cKO sciatic nerves were noticeably translucent, indicative of reduced myelin content.
source: Tead1 cKO SNs were noticeably translucent, indicative of reduced myelin content (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation shown in Figure 2B and interpretation based on established knowledge.

claim: Nerve conduction velocity in Tead1 cKO was ~8 m/s.
source: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) in cKO was ~8 m/s, which was markedly reduced from ~40 m/s in WT mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Nerve conduction velocity in WT mice was ~40 m/s.
source: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) in cKO was ~8 m/s, which was markedly reduced from ~40 m/s in WT mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Nerve conduction velocity was markedly reduced in Tead1 cKO compared to WT mice.
source: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) in cKO was ~8 m/s, which was markedly reduced from ~40 m/s in WT mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At P3, radial sorting was delayed, but not blocked, in Tead1 cKO.
source: Therefore, radial sorting was delayed, but not blocked, in Tead1 cKO.
evidence: This claim is based on TEM observations at P3 showing some sorted axons despite overall delay.

claim: At P22, Tead1 cKO sciatic nerves were largely unmyelinated.
source: At P22, when WT SNs were fully myelinated, Tead1 cKO SNs were largely unmyelinated and exhibited areas of unsorted axon bundles, of sorted but unmyelinated axons, and of thinly myelinated axons (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by semi-thin sections and TEM shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At P50, the myelination phenotype of Tead1 cKO was unchanged from that at P22.
source: Notably, at P50, this phenotype was unchanged from that at P22: areas of unsorted bundles, promyelination, and thin myelination persisted (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by semi-thin sections and TEM shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Myelin thickness did not significantly change in Tead1 cKO between P22 and P50.
source: The myelin thickness measured as g-ratio, that is, the ratio between the axon diameter and the fiber diameter (axon plus myelin sheath), did not significantly change in cKO between P22 and P50 (Figure 2H), suggesting that growth of the myelin sheath relative to axon diameter did not increase over this period.
evidence: This claim is supported by g-ratio measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Growth of the myelin sheath relative to axon diameter did not increase in Tead1 cKO between P22 and P50.
source: The myelin thickness measured as g-ratio, that is, the ratio between the axon diameter and the fiber diameter (axon plus myelin sheath), did not significantly change in cKO between P22 and P50 (Figure 2H), suggesting that growth of the myelin sheath relative to axon diameter did not increase over this period.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the g-ratio measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Myelination in Tead1 cKO was arrested rather than delayed.
source: These data suggest that myelination in Tead1 cKO was arrested rather than delayed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of change in myelin thickness between P22 and P50.

claim: The myelination defect in Tead1 cKO was present in axons of all diameters but was particularly notable in those of larger diameter.
source: Plots of g-ratio versus axon diameter showed that the mutant defect was present in axons of all diameters but was particularly notable in those of larger diameter (Figures 2I and 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by scatter plots shown in Figures 2I and 2J.

claim: The mean axon diameter was reduced in Tead1 cKO at P22.
source: The mean axon diameter was also reduced in cKO at P22, although it increased with age (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The mean axon diameter increased with age in Tead1 cKO.
source: The mean axon diameter was also reduced in cKO at P22, although it increased with age (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2K.

claim: ~80% of C-fibers were not ensheathed by Schwann cell cytoplasm in P50 Tead1 cKO sciatic nerves.
source: Quantification showed that ~80% of C-fibers were not ensheathed by SC cytoplasm in P50 Tead1 cKO SNs (Figure 2M).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2M.

claim: At P3, Schwann cell number in Tead1 cKO sciatic nerves was about half that of WT.
source: At P3, SC number in cKO SNs was about half that of WT (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The number of Schwann cells in the cell cycle was greatly reduced in Tead1 cKO at P3.
source: Consistently, the number of SCs in the cell cycle (Ki67-positive; Figure 3B) and in S-phase (EdU-positive; Figure 3C) was greatly reduced in cKO at P3.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ki67 and EdU staining shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: TEAD1 is required for optimal Schwann cell proliferation during development.
source: Thus, TEAD1 is required for optimal SC proliferation during development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduced SC proliferation at P3 in Tead1 cKO.

claim: At P22 and P50, Schwann cell numbers in Tead1 cKO were markedly increased and became more than twice those of WT.
source: Notably, at P22 and P50, SC numbers in cKO were markedly increased and became more than twice those of WT (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The number of Schwann cells that were Ki67-positive or EdU-positive was significantly increased in Tead1 cKO at P22.
source: Indeed, the number of SCs that were Ki67-positive or EdU-positive was significantly increased in cKO at P22 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ki67 and EdU staining shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The increased Schwann cell numbers in Tead1 cKO were not due to proliferation of residual Schwann cells that express TEAD1.
source: The increased SC numbers were not due to proliferation of residual SCs that express TEAD1: TEAD1 was absent in most EdU-positive SCs in Tead1 cKO (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-staining for TEAD1 and EdU shown in Figure 3D.

claim: During development, Schwann cells switch from requiring TEAD1 for optimal proliferation, to requiring TEAD1 for timely exit from the cell-cycle.
source: These data suggest that, during development, SCs switch from requiring TEAD1 for optimal proliferation, to requiring TEAD1 for timely exit from the cell-cycle, which is a prerequisite for SC differentiation and the onset of myelination (Hindley and Philpott, 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the biphasic effect of TEAD1 loss on SC proliferation at different developmental stages.

claim: Timely exit from the cell-cycle is a prerequisite for Schwann cell differentiation and the onset of myelination.
source: These data suggest that, during development, SCs switch from requiring TEAD1 for optimal proliferation, to requiring TEAD1 for timely exit from the cell-cycle, which is a prerequisite for SC differentiation and the onset of myelination (Hindley and Philpott, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: In the absence of TEAD1 in Tead1 cKO, most axons are not myelinated.
source: Our findings thus far show that, in the absence of TEAD1 in the SCs of Tead1 cKO, most axons are not myelinated, which grossly phenocopied Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO (Yap1 and Wwtr1 encode the proteins commonly listed as YAP and TAZ, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by the TEM and semi-thin section data presented earlier.

claim: The myelination phenotype of Tead1 cKO grossly phenocopied Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO.
source: Our findings thus far show that, in the absence of TEAD1 in the SCs of Tead1 cKO, most axons are not myelinated, which grossly phenocopied Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO (Yap1 and Wwtr1 encode the proteins commonly listed as YAP and TAZ, respectively).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of phenotypes between the two mutants.

claim: Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO exhibited a complete failure of myelination due to arrest of their Schwann cells as promyelinating Schwann cells.
source: Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO exhibited a complete failure of myelination due to arrest of their SCs as promyelinating SCs, in part because they fail to upregulate Krox20/Egr2 (Early Growth Response 2), which drives transcription of myelin proteins (Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO Schwann cells fail to upregulate Krox20/Egr2.
source: Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO exhibited a complete failure of myelination due to arrest of their SCs as promyelinating SCs, in part because they fail to upregulate Krox20/Egr2 (Early Growth Response 2), which drives transcription of myelin proteins (Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Oct6 expression was minimal in WT sciatic nerves at P50.
source: Western blotting of P50 SN lysates showed minimal expression of Oct6 in WT, but abnormally upregulated expression in Tead1 cKO (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Oct6 expression was abnormally upregulated in Tead1 cKO at P50.
source: Western blotting of P50 SN lysates showed minimal expression of Oct6 in WT, but abnormally upregulated expression in Tead1 cKO (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At P50, Oct6 was expressed in ~80% of Tead1 cKO Schwann cell nuclei.
source: Immunohistochemistry of P50 cKO SNs also showed intense Oct6 expression in ~80% of SC nuclei; Oct6 expression was minimal in WT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At both P11 and P50, a similar percentage of Schwann cells expressed Krox20 in Tead1 cKO as in WT sciatic nerves.
source: Notably, at both P11 and P50, a similar percentage of SCs expressed Krox20 in Tead1 cKO, as in WT SNs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Krox20 was upregulated >fourfold in Tead1 cKO compared to WT in Western blots.
source: In Western blots, Krox20 was upregulated >fourfold in cKO compared to WT (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Each Schwann cell in adult Tead1 cKO contains ~twofold more Krox20 than WT.
source: As adult Tead1 cKO mice contain ~twofold more SCs than WT (Figure 3A), these data suggest that each SC in Tead1 cKO contains ~twofold more Krox20 than WT.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blot data and SC counts.

claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20.
source: Thus, in contrast to SCs lacking YAP/TAZ, SCs lacking TEAD1 upregulate Krox20, suggesting that TEAD1 is dispensable for YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of Krox20 expression in Tead1 cKO vs Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.

claim: Expression of myelin basic protein (MBP) was abundant in WT P50 sciatic nerves.
source: Consistent with the idea that Krox20 is pivotal for myelin gene transcription, expression of myelin basic protein (MBP), and myelin protein zero (MPZ), was abundant in WT P50 SNs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of myelin protein zero (MPZ) was abundant in WT P50 sciatic nerves.
source: Consistent with the idea that Krox20 is pivotal for myelin gene transcription, expression of myelin basic protein (MBP), and myelin protein zero (MPZ), was abundant in WT P50 SNs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both MBP and MPZ were markedly decreased in Tead1 cKO despite ample expression of Krox20.
source: In contrast, despite ample expression of Krox20, both MBP and MPZ were markedly decreased in Tead1 cKO, indicating that Krox20 fails to properly upregulate myelin proteins without TEAD1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Krox20 fails to properly upregulate myelin proteins without TEAD1.
source: In contrast, despite ample expression of Krox20, both MBP and MPZ were markedly decreased in Tead1 cKO, indicating that Krox20 fails to properly upregulate myelin proteins without TEAD1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Krox20 is present but myelin proteins are reduced in Tead1 cKO.

claim: Loss of Krox20 or its co-factors, Nab1/2, causes Schwann cells to remain aberrantly in the cell-cycle.
source: To exclude the possibility that Krox20 expressed in cKO SCs is defective, we took advantage of the earlier finding that loss of Krox20 or its co-factors, Nab1/2, causes SCs to remain aberrantly in the cell-cycle (Le et al., 2005b; Zorick et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only a few EdU-positive Schwann cells exhibited even minimal Krox20 immunoreactivity in either WT or Tead1 cKO at P11.
source: We found that, although ~65% of SC nuclei contained Krox20, only a few EdU-positive SCs exhibited even minimal Krox20 immunoreactivity in either WT or Tead1 cKO (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-staining for EdU and Krox20 shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for Krox20 upregulation but required for Krox20 to upregulate transcription of myelin proteins during development.
source: Thus, despite high levels of functional Krox20, myelin protein expression was greatly reduced in cKO SCs, suggesting that TEAD1 is dispensable for Krox20 upregulation but required for Krox20 to upregulate transcription of myelin proteins during development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Krox20 is functional but myelin proteins are reduced in Tead1 cKO.

claim: De novo biosynthesis of fatty acids and cholesterol is crucially important for Schwann cells to initiate myelination and to grow a myelin sheath.
source: De novo biosynthesis of fatty acids (integral building blocks of lipids) and cholesterol is crucially important for SCs to initiate myelination and to grow a myelin sheath (Montani et al., 2018; Norrmén et al., 2014; Saher et al., 2009; Verheijen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP/TAZ may regulate lipid and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways.
source: YAP/TAZ may regulate these pathways, as suggested by reduced mRNA expression in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO of SREBPs TFs (Sterol regulatory element binding proteins) and their target enzymes involved in lipid/cholesterol biosynthesis (Deng et al., 2017; Poitelon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing reduced mRNA expression.

claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP1 were not affected by loss of TEAD1 at P8.
source: Western blot analysis showed that levels of nuclear SREBP1 were not affected by loss of TEAD1 at P8, and only slightly reduced at P40 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP1 were only slightly reduced by loss of TEAD1 at P40.
source: Western blot analysis showed that levels of nuclear SREBP1 were not affected by loss of TEAD1 at P8, and only slightly reduced at P40 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SCD1 was reduced in Tead1 cKO at P8, but slightly increased at P40.
source: SCD1 was reduced at P8, but slightly increased at P40.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SREBP2 was ~50% reduced in Tead1 cKO at both P8 and P40.
source: In contrast to SREBP1, SREBP2 was ~50% reduced in Tead1 cKO at both P8 and P40.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HMGCR was not reduced in Tead1 cKO at P8 or P40 despite marked reduction in SREBP2.
source: Despite marked reduction in SREBP2, HMGCR was not reduced at P8 or P40.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both FDPS and IDI1 levels were greatly reduced in Tead1 cKO at both P8 and P40.
source: However, both FDPS and IDI1 levels were greatly reduced at both P8 and P40 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SREBP1 levels were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
source: We found that, as in Tead1 cKO, SREBP1 levels were unaffected and SCD1 levels were markedly increased by the loss of YAP/TAZ in cDKO at P60 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SCD1 levels were markedly increased in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
source: We found that, as in Tead1 cKO, SREBP1 levels were unaffected and SCD1 levels were markedly increased by the loss of YAP/TAZ in cDKO at P60 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SREBP2 levels were not markedly reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
source: Unlike in Tead1 cKO, levels of SREBP2 were not markedly reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HMGCR levels were not reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
source: As in Tead1 cKO, however, HMGCR levels were not reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, whereas levels of FDPS and IDI1 were greatly reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Levels of FDPS and IDI1 were greatly reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
source: As in Tead1 cKO, however, HMGCR levels were not reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, whereas levels of FDPS and IDI1 were greatly reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 transcriptional complex selectively upregulates IDI1 and FDPS, contributing to cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: These results therefore indicate that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 transcriptional complex selectively upregulates IDI1 and FDPS, contributing to cholesterol biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistent reduction of FDPS and IDI1 in both Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.

claim: Reduction in cholesterol biosynthesis may prevent myelin formation and growth in Tead1 cKO.
source: Together with the lack of synthesis of myelin proteins, this reduction in cholesterol biosynthesis may prevent myelin formation and growth in Tead1 cKO.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined defects in myelin protein expression and cholesterol biosynthesis.

claim: Tead1 iKO mice appeared normal without obvious signs of peripheral neuropathy up to 5 months post-tamoxifen.
source: Tead1 iKO mice appeared normal without obvious signs of peripheral neuropathy up to 5 months post-tamoxifen, the longest time of observation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of mice.

claim: TEM analysis of Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves between 3 and 5 months post-tamoxifen revealed some large axons undergoing demyelination or completely demyelinated.
source: TEM analysis of iKO SNs between 3 and 5 months post-tamoxifen revealed, however, some large axons undergoing demyelination or completely demyelinated, which were undetectable in WT SNs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Demyelinated axons were observed in discrete regions of Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves, indicating segmental demyelination (<5% large axons).
source: The demyelinated axons were observed in discrete regions of SNs, indicating segmental demyelination (<5% large axons on 12 TEM sections exhibiting demyelinated axons).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM observations.

claim: Nerve conduction velocity of Tead1 iKO mice did not significantly differ from that of WT.
source: NCV of these iKO mice did not significantly differ from that of WT (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Loss of TEAD1 in adult Schwann cells evoked only modest focal demyelination in a small number of axons, which did not cause significant functional impairment of peripheral nerves.
source: Therefore, loss of TEAD1 in adult SCs evoked only modest focal demyelination in a small number of axons, which did not cause significant functional impairment of peripheral nerves.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TEM and NCV data in Tead1 iKO mice.

claim: Many C-fibers in most Remak bundles were not ensheathed by Schwann cell cytoplasm in Tead1 iKO.
source: In stark contrast, in Tead1 iKO, many C-fibers in most Remak bundles were not ensheathed by SC cytoplasm (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Some small Remak bundles were occasionally myelinated in Tead1 iKO.
source: Furthermore, some small Remak bundles were occasionally myelinated (Figure 6E), as in Tead1 cKO SNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TEAD1 is required for formation as well as maintenance of Remak bundles.
source: Thus, TEAD1 is required for formation as well as maintenance of Remak bundles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Remak bundle defects in both Tead1 cKO and iKO mice.

claim: Krox20 was dramatically downregulated in most Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO Schwann cells only 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: As a control, we injected Plp1-CreER; Yap1fl/fl; Wwtr1fl/fl mice with tamoxifen and reproduced our previous result: Krox20 was dramatically downregulated in most Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SCs only 2 weeks post-tamoxifen (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In Tead1 iKO, Krox20 expression was indistinguishable from WT even at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: In contrast, in Tead1 iKO, Krox20 expression was indistinguishable from WT even at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Oct6 was not elevated in Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves.
source: We then investigated Oct6 expression. Unlike in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SNs (Grove et al., 2017), Oct6 was not elevated in Tead1 iKO SNs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for maintaining Krox20 expression in adult Schwann cells.
source: Thus, TEAD1 is dispensable for maintaining Krox20 expression in adult SCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the normal Krox20 expression in Tead1 iKO.

claim: The SREBP1 pathway was unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO at 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: Western blotting of WT and Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SN lysates showed that the SREBP1 pathway and expression of SREBP2 and HMGCR in the SREBP2 pathway were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Expression of SREBP2 and HMGCR in the SREBP2 pathway were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO at 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: Western blotting of WT and Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SN lysates showed that the SREBP1 pathway and expression of SREBP2 and HMGCR in the SREBP2 pathway were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: FDPS and IDI1 levels were significantly downregulated in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO at 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: However, FDPS and IDI1 levels were significantly downregulated in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO, recapitulating the effect of developmental loss of YAP/TAZ on these proteins (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The acute downregulation of FDPS and IDI1 correlates with the acute demyelination previously observed in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice.
source: Thus, the acute downregulation of these key enzymes for cholesterol biosynthesis correlates with the acute demyelination previously observed in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between enzyme downregulation and demyelination phenotype.

claim: YAP/TAZ maintain myelination through both myelin gene expression and the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway.
source: This result suggests that YAP/TAZ maintain myelination through both myelin gene expression and the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the effects of YAP/TAZ loss on both Krox20 and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.

claim: The SREBP pathways were not significantly affected by loss of TEAD1 in adult Schwann cells.
source: Western blotting of Tead1 iKO SN lysates revealed that the SREBP pathways were not significantly affected by loss of TEAD1 (Figure 7E), unlike Tead1 cKO in which FDPS and IDI1 were markedly downregulated (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for cholesterol synthesis in adult Schwann cells.
source: This result suggests that TEAD1 is dispensable for cholesterol synthesis in adult SCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of effect on SREBP pathways in Tead1 iKO.

claim: YAP/TAZ are not required for axon regeneration but are crucial for remyelination.
source: YAP/TAZ are not required for axon regeneration but are crucial for remyelination (Grove et al., 2017; Jeanette et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice die ~2 weeks post-injury.
source: Because Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice die ~2 weeks post-injury (wpi), it remains possible that remyelination is delayed rather than completely blocked.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Numerous Tuj1-labeled axons regenerated along the distal nerve stump in Tead1 iKO, as in WT sciatic nerves.
source: Longitudinal sections of iKO SNs showed numerous Tuj1-labeled axons that regenerated along the distal nerve stump, as in WT SNs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: MBP immunoreactivity was greatly reduced in the distal nerve stump of Tead1 iKO compared to WT.
source: However, MBP immunoreactivity was greatly reduced in the distal nerve stump of Tead1 iKO, compared to WT, suggesting that axons regenerated but were not remyelinated.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Axons regenerated but were not remyelinated in Tead1 iKO after nerve crush.
source: However, MBP immunoreactivity was greatly reduced in the distal nerve stump of Tead1 iKO, compared to WT, suggesting that axons regenerated but were not remyelinated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of axons but absence of myelin in Tead1 iKO.

claim: Regenerated axons reached hindlimb muscles and reinnervated neuromuscular junctions in Tead1 iKO, as in WT.
source: We also found that regenerated axons reached hindlimb muscles and reinnervated neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) in iKO, as in WT (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ staining shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tead1 iKO frequently exhibited features of paralyzed muscles after nerve crush.
source: Moreover, Tead1 iKO frequently exhibited features of paralyzed muscles, such as axon terminals that grew past the synaptic area, fragmented clusters of acetylcholine receptors (AChRs), and satellite extra-synaptic AChRs (Wright et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ staining shown in Figure 8C and citation to previous work.

claim: Semithin and EM analysis confirmed virtual absence of myelinated axons in Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves after nerve crush.
source: Semithin and EM analysis confirmed virtual absence of myelinated axons in iKO SNs; although large axons were associated with SCs, they were not myelinated (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by semi-thin and TEM data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Electrical stimulation of Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves did not elicit CMAPs or NCV after nerve crush.
source: Accordingly, electrical stimulation of iKO SNs did not elicit CMAPs or NCV (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: TEAD1 in Schwann cells is not required for axon regeneration but is required for remyelination after nerve injury.
source: Thus, like YAP/TAZ, TEAD1 in SCs is not required for axon regeneration but is required for remyelination after nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the nerve crush experiments in Tead1 iKO mice.

claim: A similar percentage of Schwann cells were in S-phase in both WT and Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves at 3 days post-injury.
source: Quantitative analysis of SC proliferation at 3 dpi by counting EdU+/Sox10+ SCs showed that a similar percentage of SCs were in S-phase in both WT and Tead1 iKO SNs (Figure 8F), suggesting that, like YAP/TAZ (Grove et al., 2017), TEAD1 is not required for proliferation of repair SCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU staining shown in Figure 8F.

claim: TEAD1 is not required for proliferation of repair Schwann cells.
source: Quantitative analysis of SC proliferation at 3 dpi by counting EdU+/Sox10+ SCs showed that a similar percentage of SCs were in S-phase in both WT and Tead1 iKO SNs (Figure 8F), suggesting that, like YAP/TAZ (Grove et al., 2017), TEAD1 is not required for proliferation of repair SCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar proliferation rates in WT and Tead1 iKO after injury.

claim: Krox20 was upregulated in Tead1 iKO Schwann cells at 4 weeks post-injury, as in WT Schwann cells.
source: Notably, in contrast to Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SCs, which fail to upregulate Krox20 after injury (Grove et al., 2017), Krox20 was upregulated in Tead1 iKO SCs, as in WT SCs (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Oct6 was aberrantly elevated in Tead1 iKO Schwann cells at 4 weeks post-injury.
source: Furthermore, Oct6 was aberrantly elevated in Tead1 iKO SCs, like in Tead1 cKO SCs during development (Figure 8H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Remyelination requires TEAD1 for Oct6 downregulation and for Krox20 to upregulate myelin proteins.
source: These results suggest that, similar to developmental myelination, remyelination requires TEAD1 for Oct6 downregulation and for Krox20 to upregulate myelin proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of molecular phenotypes between developmental and regenerative myelination in Tead1 mutants.

claim: Almost complete absence of remyelination at 4 weeks post-injury highlights the non-redundant, crucial role of TEAD1 in the remyelination of regenerating nerves after injury.
source: Additionally, almost complete absence of remyelination at 4 wpi highlights the non-redundant, crucial role of TEAD1 in the remyelination of regenerating nerves after injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the severe remyelination defect in Tead1 iKO after nerve crush.

claim: TEAD1 is a crucial transcription factor mediating myelin formation, growth, and regeneration.
source: The present study conclusively establishes TEAD1 as a crucial TF mediating myelin formation, growth, and regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEAD1 is critical in the proper formation and maintenance of Remak bundles.
source: Our findings also suggest that TEAD1 is critical in the proper formation and maintenance of Remak bundles.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the Remak bundle data in Tead1 cKO and iKO mice.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice grossly phenocopy Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO mice.
source: Although SCs express other TEADs, Tead1 cKO mice grossly phenocopy Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO mice.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of phenotypes between the two mutants.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit abnormal Schwann cell proliferation.
source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary of the proliferation data presented earlier.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit delayed radial sorting.
source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary of the radial sorting data presented earlier.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit blocked myelin formation and remyelination.
source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary of the myelination data presented earlier.

claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit normal axon regeneration.
source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary of the axon regeneration data presented earlier.

claim: YAP/TAZ regulate both Schwann cell proliferation and differentiation by partnering mainly with TEAD1 for developmental myelination and remyelination after injury.
source: These similarities show that YAP/TAZ regulate both SC proliferation and differentiation, the two opposing processes crucial for myelination, by partnering mainly with TEAD1 for developmental myelination and remyelination after injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.

claim: Unlike Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, Tead1 cKO initiates myelin formation in some developing axons.
source: Unlike Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, Tead1 cKO initiates myelin formation in some developing axons and maintains myelination in almost all adult axons.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of myelination phenotypes between the two mutants.

claim: Tead1 cKO maintains myelination in almost all adult axons.
source: Unlike Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, Tead1 cKO initiates myelin formation in some developing axons and maintains myelination in almost all adult axons.
evidence: This claim is based on the Tead1 iKO data showing minimal demyelination.

claim: In Tead1 cKO, Krox20 is upregulated and a large excess of Schwann cells is generated.
source: Additionally, in Tead1 cKO, Krox20 is upregulated and a large excess of SCs is generated.
evidence: This is a summary of the Krox20 and SC number data presented earlier.

claim: Whereas some developing axons are myelinated in Tead1 cKO, almost all axons regenerating after injury are unmyelinated.
source: It is also notable that, whereas some developing axons are myelinated in Tead1 cKO, almost all axons regenerating after injury are unmyelinated.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of developmental and regenerative myelination in Tead1 cKO.

claim: The differences between Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO are likely due to stage-dependent redundancy and opposing roles of TEADs.
source: These differences are likely due to stage-dependent redundancy and opposing roles of TEADs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotypic differences and the known expression of multiple TEADs.

claim: Other TEADs can retain nuclear YAP/TAZ, thereby supporting transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ, but cannot substitute for some or most of the functions of TEAD1 in a stage-dependent manner.
source: Thus, other TEADs can retain nuclear YAP/TAZ, thereby supporting transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ, but cannot substitute for some or most of the functions of TEAD1 in a stage-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ in Tead1 mutants and the phenotypic differences from Yap1/Wwtr1 mutants.

claim: The unique roles of TEAD1 change dynamically in successive steps of myelination, even though other TEADs are present.
source: It is also notable that, like YAP/TAZ, the unique roles of TEAD1 change dynamically in successive steps of myelination, even though other TEADs are present.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the different phenotypes at different developmental stages.

claim: TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of Schwann cells.
source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: This is a summary of the proliferation data at P3.

claim: TEAD1 uniquely opposes Schwann cell proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting.
source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: This is a summary of the proliferation data at P22.

claim: TEAD1 redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20.
source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: This is a summary of the Krox20 data showing normal upregulation in Tead1 cKO.

claim: TEAD1 uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: This is a summary of the myelin protein and cholesterol biosynthesis data.

claim: YAP-TEAD4 can substitute for YAP-TEAD1 in upregulating transcription from the Krox20 promoter, but not from the MPZ intronic enhancer.
source: Such unique and redundant roles for TEAD1 in the presence of other TEADs are supported by cell-based transcription assays, in which YAP-TEAD4 can substitute for YAP-TEAD1 in upregulating transcription from the Krox20 promoter, but not from the MPZ intronic enhancer (Fernando et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous cell-based transcription assays.

claim: Stage-dependent function of TEADs was reported in cortical development.
source: Stage-dependent function of TEADs was also reported in cortical development, another multi-step differentiation program.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge from other systems.

claim: In cortical development, multiple TEADs (TEAD1-3) are co-expressed throughout development.
source: As in nerve development, multiple TEADs (TEAD1-3) are co-expressed throughout cortical development.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge from cortical development studies.

claim: In cortical development, depending on the differentiation stage, TEAD1 uniquely promotes proliferation, redundantly promotes proliferation with TEAD2 and 3, or redundantly promotes differentiation with TEAD3, when it is opposed by TEAD2.
source: Depending on the differentiation stage, TEAD1 uniquely promotes proliferation, redundantly promotes proliferation with TEAD2 and 3, or redundantly promotes differentiation with TEAD3, when it is opposed by TEAD2 (Mukhtar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study on cortical development.

claim: Some Tead1 cKO Schwann cells can myelinate but fail to grow myelin sheaths proportional in size to axon diameter.
source: In contrast, some Tead1 cKO SCs can myelinate but fail to grow myelin sheaths proportional in size to axon diameter.
evidence: This is a summary of the g-ratio data presented earlier.

claim: Such myelinating Schwann cells in Tead1 cKO apparently lack TEAD1 because TEAD1 deletion is highly efficient in Tead1 cKO mice.
source: Importantly, such myelinating SCs apparently lack TEAD1 because TEAD1 deletion is highly efficient in Tead1 cKO mice.
evidence: This claim is based on the high efficiency of TEAD1 deletion shown in Figure 1.

claim: In TEAD4 cKO mice, Schwann cells lacking TEAD4 gradually upregulate myelin protein expression, resulting in adult mice with abnormally thick myelin.
source: Support for a role of TEADs in the regulation of myelin sheath thickness comes from a study of TEAD4 cKO mice, in which SCs lacking TEAD4 gradually upregulate myelin protein expression, resulting in adult mice with abnormally thick myelin (He et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study on TEAD4 cKO mice.

claim: It is possible that TEADs 1 and 4 oppose each other in the regulation of myelin sheath growth.
source: Thus, it is possible that TEADs 1 and 4 oppose each other in the regulation of myelin sheath growth.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the opposite phenotypes of TEAD1 and TEAD4 mutants.

claim: TEADs 1 and 4 may oppose each other in the regulation of Schwann cell proliferation during development, resulting in a large excess of Schwann cells at P22 and P50 in Tead1 cKO.
source: Likewise, they may oppose each other in the regulation of SC proliferation during development, resulting in a large excess of SCs at P22 and P50 in Tead1 cKO.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the excess SC phenotype in Tead1 cKO.

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 promote myelination in part through direct upregulation of Krox20.
source: Previous work suggests that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 promote myelination in part through direct upregulation of Krox20 (Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TEAD1 functions redundantly in direct upregulation of Krox20.
source: Our findings extend previous work to suggest that TEAD1 functions redundantly in direct upregulation of Krox20, but that its function is required for upregulated Krox20 to promote myelination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the normal Krox20 upregulation in Tead1 cKO.

claim: TEAD1 function is required for upregulated Krox20 to promote myelination.
source: Our findings extend previous work to suggest that TEAD1 functions redundantly in direct upregulation of Krox20, but that its function is required for upregulated Krox20 to promote myelination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the failure of myelin protein upregulation despite Krox20 presence in Tead1 cKO.

claim: Krox20 activity may be repressed in Tead1 cKO by Oct6, which remains abnormally elevated.
source: Krox20 activity may be repressed in Tead1 cKO by Oct6, which remains abnormally elevated.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the elevated Oct6 and reduced myelin proteins in Tead1 cKO.

claim: Persistently elevated Oct6 overrides Krox20 to inhibit myelin gene expression.
source: In support of this possibility, persistently elevated Oct6 overrides Krox20 to inhibit myelin gene expression (Monuki et al., 1993; Ryu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Other mice with defective lipid biosynthesis and a phenotype like Tead1 cKO also have abnormally elevated Oct6 after Krox20 upregulation.
source: Other mice with defective lipid biosynthesis and a phenotype like Tead1 cKO also have abnormally elevated Oct6 after Krox20 upregulation (Norrmén et al., 2014; Sherman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A transcriptional co-activator that synergizes with Krox20 may be absent in Tead1 cKO Schwann cells.
source: An alternative possibility is that a transcriptional co-activator that synergizes with Krox20 is absent in Tead1 cKO SCs.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the myelin protein defect.

claim: TEAD1 itself may function as a transcriptional co-activator that synergizes with Krox20.
source: We speculate that TEAD1 itself may function as such a factor.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Gene regulatory elements function by co-binding several transcription factors, which synergistically activate transcription.
source: Supporting this idea are reports that gene regulatory elements function by co-binding several TFs, which synergistically activate transcription (Heinz et al., 2015; Ren and Yue, 2015), as at the Krox20 MSE (Myelinating Schwann cell element) which is the enhancer responsible for Krox20 expression (Ghislain and Charnay, 2006; Grove et al., 2017; He et al., 2010; Kao et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Krox20 synergizes with Sox10 to activate myelin genes.
source: Krox20 synergizes with Sox10 to activate myelin genes (Jones et al., 2007) and with SREBP to activate lipid biosynthesis genes (Leblanc et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Krox20 synergizes with SREBP to activate lipid biosynthesis genes.
source: Krox20 synergizes with Sox10 to activate myelin genes (Jones et al., 2007) and with SREBP to activate lipid biosynthesis genes (Leblanc et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TEAD1 can directly promote transcription from PMP22 and MPZ myelin gene enhancers.
source: Like Krox20, TEAD1 can directly promote transcription from PMP22 and MPZ myelin gene enhancers (Fernando et al., 2016; Lopez-Anido et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TEAD1 may function indirectly by upregulating co-factors, such as SREBP2, which is reduced in Tead1 cKO.
source: Alternatively, or additionally, TEAD1 may function indirectly by upregulating co-factors, such as SREBP2, which is reduced in Tead1 cKO.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on the SREBP2 data.

claim: Lipid biosynthesis is necessary to downregulate Oct6 and upregulate myelin gene transcription during developmental myelination.
source: Notably, lipid biosynthesis is necessary to downregulate Oct6 and upregulate myelin gene transcription during developmental myelination (Saher et al., 2009; Verheijen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 and Krox20 may cooperatively downregulate Oct6 and upregulate myelin gene expression in part by promoting lipid biosynthesis.
source: An interesting possibility, therefore, is that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 and Krox20 may cooperatively downregulate Oct6 and upregulate myelin gene expression in part by promoting lipid biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis integrating multiple observations.

claim: Fatty acid synthesis is not directly regulated by TEAD1 or YAP/TAZ.
source: SREBP1 levels are not altered in Tead1 cKO or Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, suggesting that fatty acid synthesis is not directly regulated by TEAD1 or YAP/TAZ.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of effect on SREBP1 levels.

claim: The reduced levels of SCD1 at P8 and slight increase at P40 in Tead1 cKO, and the large increase in SCD1 in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60 are likely due to developmental delay in these mutants.
source: It is likely that the reduced levels of SCD1 at P8 and slight increase at P40 in Tead1 cKO, and the large increase in SCD1 in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60 are due to developmental delay in these mutants.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the developmental delay phenotype of the mutants.

claim: Marked downregulation of IDI1 and FDPS in Tead1 cKO, Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, and Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO suggests that cholesterol biosynthesis is defective in these mutants.
source: However, marked downregulation of IDI1 and FDPS in Tead1 cKO, Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, and Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO suggests that cholesterol biosynthesis is defective in these mutants.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the enzyme downregulation data.

claim: SC-selective deletion of SCAP evokes phenotypes which are remarkably similar to those of Tead1 cKO mice.
source: In support of this notion, SC-selective deletion of SCAP (SREBP cleavage activation protein), which is required to produce active SREBP1 and SREBP2 (Verheijen et al., 2009), or of Squalene synthase, an essential enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis (Saher et al., 2009), evokes phenotypes which are remarkably similar to those of Tead1 cKO mice: both mutants have an increased number of SCs, a severe delay at the promyelination stage, and persistently thin myelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of Squalene synthase evokes phenotypes which are remarkably similar to those of Tead1 cKO mice.
source: In support of this notion, SC-selective deletion of SCAP (SREBP cleavage activation protein), which is required to produce active SREBP1 and SREBP2 (Verheijen et al., 2009), or of Squalene synthase, an essential enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis (Saher et al., 2009), evokes phenotypes which are remarkably similar to those of Tead1 cKO mice: both mutants have an increased number of SCs, a severe delay at the promyelination stage, and persistently thin myelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In SCAP cKO, Oct6 is upregulated continuously.
source: In addition, in SCAP cKO, Oct6 is upregulated continuously and Squalene synthase cKO fails to upregulate myelin gene transcription, resulting in severely reduced MBP, MPZ, and PMP22 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Squalene synthase cKO fails to upregulate myelin gene transcription, resulting in severely reduced MBP, MPZ, and PMP22 protein levels.
source: In addition, in SCAP cKO, Oct6 is upregulated continuously and Squalene synthase cKO fails to upregulate myelin gene transcription, resulting in severely reduced MBP, MPZ, and PMP22 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: YAP/TAZ can activate the mTORC1 pathway.
source: Multiple studies show that YAP/TAZ can activate the mTORC1 pathway (Hu et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2015), and that IDI1 and FDPS levels are reduced in SNs of Raptor cKO, a core component of mTORC1 (Norrmén et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: IDI1 and FDPS levels are reduced in sciatic nerves of Raptor cKO.
source: Multiple studies show that YAP/TAZ can activate the mTORC1 pathway (Hu et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2015), and that IDI1 and FDPS levels are reduced in SNs of Raptor cKO, a core component of mTORC1 (Norrmén et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The Raptor cKO phenotype is like that of Tead1 cKO, exhibiting an increased number of Schwann cells, normal upregulation of Krox20, persistent upregulation of Oct6, delay at the promyelination stage, and thin myelin.
source: Furthermore, the Raptor cKO phenotype is like that of Tead1 cKO, exhibiting an increased number of SCs, normal upregulation of Krox20, persistent upregulation of Oct6, delay at the promyelination stage, and thin myelin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In Raptor cKO, HMGCR protein levels are reduced, and aberrant upregulation of Oct6 is transient.
source: However, HMGCR protein levels are reduced, and aberrant upregulation of Oct6 is transient (Norrmén et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: After nerve injury, formation of repair Schwann cells is delayed in Raptor mutants.
source: After nerve injury, formation of repair SCs is delayed in Raptor mutants (Norrmén et al., 2018), unlike TEAD1 and YAP/TAZ mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The differences between Raptor cKO and Tead1 cKO suggest that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 are not directly upstream of mTORC1.
source: These differences suggest that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 are not directly upstream of mTORC1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotypic differences between Raptor cKO and Tead1 cKO.

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 may directly regulate transcription of IDI1 and FDPS genes.
source: Another possibility is that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 may directly regulate transcription of IDI1 and FDPS genes.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism.

claim: Direct regulation of cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes has been observed for other transcription factors in Schwann cells.
source: Such direct regulation of cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes has been observed for other TFs in SCs (Kim et al., 2018; Leblanc et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The defective Schwann cell ensheathment of C-fibers observed in Tead1 cKO and iKO is distinct from radial sorting defects.
source: This phenotype is distinct from those mutants in which SCs surround and occasionally myelinate bundles filled with large and small caliber axons, which are considered radial sorting defects (Feltri et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with other mutants and citation to previous work.

claim: Remak bundles are occasionally myelinated in WT sciatic nerves during early postnatal development, but this defect is corrected and does not persist in adults.
source: Remak bundles are occasionally myelinated in WT SNs during early postnatal development, but this defect is corrected and does not persist in adults (Rasi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The defective Remak bundles observed in Tead1 cKO are not due to developmental delay.
source: Thus, the defective Remak bundles that we observed in Tead1 cKO are not due to developmental delay.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the persistence of the defect and comparison with WT development.

claim: Remak bundles form normally at P60 in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.
source: Remak bundles form normally at P60 in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, although many large bundles containing mixed caliber axons are present during development (Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The difference in Remak bundle phenotype between Tead1 and Yap1/Wwtr1 mutants is supported by the presence of TEAD1 and absence of YAP/TAZ in non-myelinating Schwann cell nuclei.
source: The difference between Tead1 and Yap1/Wwtr1 mutants is supported by the presence of TEAD1 and absence of YAP/TAZ in non-myelinating SC nuclei (Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Defective Schwann cell ensheathment of C-fibers is observed in various Schwann cell developmental mutants, including those with defective Schwann cell basal lamina.
source: Notably, defective SC ensheathment of C-fibers is observed in various SC developmental mutants, including those with defective SC basal lamina (Rasi et al., 2010) and overexpression of NRG1-IIIb (Neuregulin 1 type-IIIb) in axons (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Defective Schwann cell ensheathment of C-fibers is observed in mutants with overexpression of NRG1-IIIb in axons.
source: Notably, defective SC ensheathment of C-fibers is observed in various SC developmental mutants, including those with defective SC basal lamina (Rasi et al., 2010) and overexpression of NRG1-IIIb (Neuregulin 1 type-IIIb) in axons (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TEAD1 may mediate extracellular signaling from the Schwann cell basal lamina and/or axons that is responsible for forming and maintaining proper association of Schwann cells with C-fibers.
source: Therefore, it is possible that TEAD1 mediates extracellular signaling from the SC basal lamina and/or axons that is responsible for forming and maintaining proper association of SCs with C-fibers.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the Remak bundle phenotype and comparison with other mutants.

claim: Schwann cell ensheathment of C-fibers is required for normal nerve conduction velocity.
source: Notably, SC ensheathment of C-fibers is required for normal NCV (Taveggia et al., 2005), and NCV in the mutants overexpressing NRG1-IIIb is significantly reduced compared to WT (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nerve conduction velocity in mutants overexpressing NRG1-IIIb is significantly reduced compared to WT.
source: Notably, SC ensheathment of C-fibers is required for normal NCV (Taveggia et al., 2005), and NCV in the mutants overexpressing NRG1-IIIb is significantly reduced compared to WT (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Mpz-Cre is active from E13.5 in Schwann cells.
source: Targeted ablation of Tead1 in Schwann cells of embryonic mice was achieved by crossing Tead1fl/fl mice with mice transgenic for Cre driven by the Mpz promoter (Tead1 cKO mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Mpz-Cre mice.
